title: 07. Advanced & Agentic RAG: MCP Primitives: Tools (The Most Important One)
summary: In the last lesson we learned how messages travel. Today we learn the most important thing you will build: Tools — the functions your AI agent can call.
objectives: ① Real-World Analogy — The Swiss Army Knife

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: **In the last lesson** we learned how messages travel. **Today** we learn the most important thing you will build: **Tools** — the functions your AI agent can call.

sections.title: ① Real-World Analogy — The Swiss Army Knife
sections.body:
An MCP Tool is like one blade on a Swiss Army knife. Each blade (tool) does one specific thing:
- The knife blade = `read_file` tool
- The scissors = `search_web` tool
- The bottle opener = `send_email` tool

When the AI agent needs to do something, it looks at all available blades and picks the right one. The label on each blade (the tool's **description**) is what the AI reads to decide which one to use.

If the label is unclear ("blade-thing"), the AI might pick the wrong one. If the label is clear ("cuts paper, fabric, and string"), the AI knows exactly when to use it. **That is why tool descriptions are so critical.**

sections.title: ② Plain English Explanation
sections.body:
An MCP Tool is a Python function that:
1. Has a **name** (so the AI can refer to it)
2. Has a **description** (so the AI knows what it does)
3. Has **defined inputs** (so the AI knows what to send it)
4. Returns a **result** (the answer the AI uses in its response)

When you register a tool with an MCP server, you are essentially saying: "Hey AI, here is a function you are allowed to call. Here is what it does, here is what you need to give it, and here is what you will get back."

sections.title: ③ Why Does This Matter?
sections.body:
Without tools, an AI agent is like a very smart person locked in a room with no phone, no computer, and no windows — they can reason and write, but they cannot **do** anything. Tools are the doors out of that room.

Every practical AI application (ChatGPT plugins, Claude agents, LangChain agents) is built on the concept of tools. MCP just standardizes how you define and expose them.

sections.title: ④ Step-by-Step Technical Explanation
sections.body:
### The Anatomy of an MCP Tool

Every MCP tool has these parts:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TOOL ANATOMY                                               │
│                                                             │
│  name:        "add_numbers"                                 │
│  ↑ What the AI calls when it wants this tool                │
│                                                             │
│  description: "Add two integers together. Returns the sum." │
│  ↑ What the AI reads to decide IF to use this tool          │
│    THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT FIELD — write it clearly!     │
│                                                             │
│  inputSchema: {                                             │
│    type: "object",                                          │
│    properties: {                                            │
│      a: { type: "integer", description: "First number" },   │
│      b: { type: "integer", description: "Second number" }   │
│    },                                                       │
│    required: ["a", "b"]                                     │
│  }                                                          │
│  ↑ The shape of the inputs the AI must provide              │
│    Written in JSON Schema format                            │
│                                                             │
│  handler:     async def add_numbers(a, b): return a + b     │
│  ↑ Your actual Python function that runs when called        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### JSON Schema — Simple Explanation

JSON Schema is just a way to describe what shape your data should be. Think of it as a form with fields:

```
JSON Schema:                    Like a form that says:
──────────────────────          ──────────────────────────────────
{                               ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  "type": "object",             │  FORM: add_numbers           │
  "properties": {               │  ┌──────────────────────┐   │
    "a": {                      │  │ First number:  [    ] │   │
      "type": "integer",        │  │  (must be whole num)  │   │
      "description": "First     │  └──────────────────────┘   │
                      number"   │  ┌──────────────────────┐   │
    },                          │  │ Second number: [    ] │   │
    "b": {                      │  │  (must be whole num)  │   │
      "type": "integer",        │  └──────────────────────┘   │
      "description": "Second    │  * both fields required      │
                      number"   └──────────────────────────────┘
    }
  },
  "required": ["a", "b"]
}
```

Common JSON Schema types you will use:

```
"type": "string"   → Any text: "hello", "world"
"type": "integer"  → Whole numbers: 1, 42, -5
"type": "number"   → Any number including decimals: 3.14, -0.5
"type": "boolean"  → True or false
"type": "array"    → A list: [1, 2, 3] or ["a", "b"]
"type": "object"   → A dictionary: {"key": "value"}
```

### Tool Return Types

Your tool can return different types of content:

```python
# Return simple text
return "Hello, world!"

# Return a number (gets converted to text automatically by MCP SDK)
return 42

# Return structured content (for richer responses)
return [TextContent(type="text", text="The answer is 8")]

# Return an error
raise ValueError("Something went wrong")  # MCP catches this and sends error response
```

sections.title: ⑤ Beginner-Friendly Code Example
sections.body:
Let us build a complete MCP tool step by step.

**Step 1 — The absolute minimum tool:**

```python
# step1_minimal_tool.py
# Install first: pip install fastmcp

from fastmcp import FastMCP   # The easy-to-use MCP library

mcp = FastMCP("Calculator")   # Create our server, name it "Calculator"

@mcp.tool()                   # This decorator registers the function as a tool
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two numbers together and return the result."""
    return a + b              # Just a normal Python function!

# That is it! FastMCP reads:
# - The function name ("add") → becomes the tool name
# - The docstring → becomes the tool description
# - The type hints (int, int → int) → becomes the JSON Schema automatically
```

**Step 2 — Let us see what JSON Schema FastMCP generates:**

```python
# step2_inspect_schema.py
# Let us see what FastMCP automatically creates for us

from fastmcp import FastMCP
import asyncio

mcp = FastMCP("Calculator")

@mcp.tool()
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two numbers together and return the result."""
    return a + b

@mcp.tool()
def greet(name: str, formal: bool = False) -> str:
    """
    Greet a person by name.
    name:   The person's name
    formal: If True, use formal greeting (Mr./Ms.). Default is False.
    """
    if formal:
        return f"Good day, Mr./Ms. {name}."
    return f"Hey {name}!"

# Let us inspect what the tools look like to the AI
async def inspect_tools():
    """Show the tools as the AI client would see them"""
    tools = await mcp.list_tools()     # Get all registered tools
    
    for tool in tools:
        print(f"\n{'='*50}")
        print(f"Tool Name:    {tool.name}")
        print(f"Description:  {tool.description}")
        print(f"Input Schema: ")
        
        import json
        schema_str = json.dumps(tool.inputSchema, indent=2)  # Pretty print the schema
        for line in schema_str.split('\n'):
            print(f"              {line}")   # Indent each line for readability

# Run the inspection
asyncio.run(inspect_tools())
```

**Expected output:**

```
==================================================
Tool Name:    add
Description:  Add two numbers together and return the result.
Input Schema: 
              {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                  "a": {
                    "type": "integer",
                    "description": "a"
                  },
                  "b": {
                    "type": "integer",
                    "description": "b"
                  }
                },
                "required": [
                  "a",
                  "b"
                ]
              }

==================================================
Tool Name:    greet
Description:  Greet a person by name.
              name:   The person's name
              formal: If True, use formal greeting...
Input Schema: 
              {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                  "name": {
                    "type": "string",
                    "description": "name"
                  },
                  "formal": {
                    "type": "boolean",
                    "description": "formal",
                    "default": false
                  }
                },
                "required": [
                  "name"
                ]
              }
```

**Step 3 — Now let us build the complete calculator with all operations:**

```python
# step3_full_calculator.py
# A complete calculator MCP server with four operations
# Run with: python step3_full_calculator.py

from fastmcp import FastMCP   # Easy MCP library

# Create our MCP server
mcp = FastMCP(
    name="Calculator Server",          # Human-readable name
    instructions="A simple calculator that can add, subtract, multiply, and divide numbers."
    # Instructions tell the AI how to use this server overall
)

@mcp.tool()
def add(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """
    Add two numbers together.
    
    a: The first number (can be decimal, e.g. 3.14)
    b: The second number (can be decimal, e.g. 2.5)
    
    Returns: The sum of a and b
    """
    result = a + b                     # Do the math
    print(f"Tool called: add({a}, {b}) = {result}")  # Log to stderr in production
    return result                      # Return the answer

@mcp.tool()
def subtract(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """
    Subtract b from a.
    
    a: The number to subtract from
    b: The number to subtract
    
    Returns: a minus b
    """
    result = a - b
    return result

@mcp.tool()
def multiply(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """
    Multiply two numbers together.
    
    a: The first number
    b: The second number
    
    Returns: The product of a and b
    """
    result = a * b
    return result

@mcp.tool()
def divide(a: float, b: float) -> str:
    """
    Divide a by b. Returns an error message if b is zero.
    
    a: The number to divide (the dividend)
    b: The number to divide by (the divisor) — must not be zero
    
    Returns: The result as text, or an error message if division by zero
    """
    # ALWAYS validate inputs before doing anything with them
    if b == 0:
        # We return a string error message — the AI can read this and explain it
        return "Error: Cannot divide by zero. Please provide a non-zero divisor."
    
    result = a / b
    return str(round(result, 6))   # Round to 6 decimal places for cleanliness

# Run the server (stdio transport by default)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Starting Calculator MCP Server...", file=__import__('sys').stderr)
    mcp.run()   # Default transport is stdio
```

sections.title: ⑥ Common Beginner Mistakes
sections.body:
```
❌ Mistake 1: Writing a vague tool description
   Example: description="This tool does stuff"
   Why it happens: Developers think the code is self-explanatory
   ✅ Fix: Write descriptions as if explaining to someone who cannot see your code.
         "Add two numbers together. Returns the integer sum. Use this when
          the user asks to add, sum, or calculate a total."

❌ Mistake 2: Not handling errors in the tool
   Example: def divide(a, b): return a/b  (crashes when b=0)
   Why it happens: Forgetting that AI will call tools with unexpected values
   ✅ Fix: Always validate inputs. Return error strings or raise ValueError
         with a clear message rather than letting the function crash.

❌ Mistake 3: Forgetting type hints
   Example: def add(a, b):  (no types!)
   Why it happens: Python does not require type hints
   ✅ Fix: FastMCP NEEDS type hints to build the JSON Schema.
         Without them, the tool has no schema and AI cannot call it properly.

❌ Mistake 4: Making tools that do too many things
   Example: def handle_everything(action, data, type, mode, config)
   Why it happens: Trying to minimize the number of tools
   ✅ Fix: One tool = one clear action. Small, focused tools work much better.
         AI agents are much better at picking the right tool from many
         specific tools than picking the right "mode" of one giant tool.

❌ Mistake 5: Using print() for tool output
   Example: def add(a, b): print(a + b)  (no return statement!)
   Why it happens: Python programmers often print results
   ✅ Fix: Always use "return" — not "print()". The return value is what
         the MCP framework sends back to the AI client.
```

sections.title: ⑦ Quick Recap — What Did We Just Learn?
sections.body:
- ✅ A Tool = a Python function the AI agent can call remotely
- ✅ Tools need: name, description (CRITICAL), input schema, and a return value
- ✅ FastMCP reads your Python type hints to build JSON Schema automatically
- ✅ Always validate inputs — the AI might send unexpected values
- ✅ One tool = one clear action — keep tools focused and specific
